description:
## Question

Ash uses a SAT solver to check policy and filter satisfiability, with two interchangeable backends on Hex: simple_sat (pure Elixir, https://github.com/ash-project/simple_sat) and picosat_elixir (a NIF over PicoSAT, https://fmv.jku.at/picosat/, a ~7k-line C CDCL solver). That is the catalog's ideal shape: a real job, a pure-Elixir baseline and a hand-written-NIF comparison that already coexist. Decide whether it is a good defk example, and in which form:
(a) simple_sat's job: the formulas Ash actually solves (how many variables and clauses, how many calls per request, DPLL vs CDCL in simple_sat's code), measured on simple_sat vs picosat_elixir; is the per-call size so small that the boundary dominates (poor_tiny_calls lesson), or is there a batch form?
(b) a picosat-style reimplementation: what a CDCL solver needs from the kernel subset. Clause database in CSR form over [i64] (literals, clause offsets), watched-literal lists, a trail with decision levels, VSIDS activity (f64 array plus a heap over arrays), conflict analysis producing learned clauses (data-dependent growth: how big can the learned-clause store be bounded, or does it need defk-cmr-style growable output or kernel-owned state, defk-sve), restarts, iterative DPLL/CDCL with explicit stacks (no recursion in the subset), and early exit. Which of these the subset has today, which are ticketed (defk-w38 bitwise, defk-n4r.4 writable helper arrays, defk-n4r.3 slices, defk-ivt constants, defk-cmr, defk-sve), and what is new.
(c) The one rule: a solver is deterministic given the same algorithm and tie-breaks, so Elixir mode can agree exactly; but result equivalence for SAT is "same satisfiability and a valid model", not "identical model", unless the algorithm is pinned. State what the agreement property should compare.
(d) Scheduling: picosat_elixir runs on normal schedulers? (check its NIF flags) and hard instances take seconds, so the yield story applies.

Output: a ranked recommendation (simple_sat's job as a target workload with anchors simple_sat and picosat_elixir; a bounded CDCL kernel as a Tier 2/3 rewrite; or neither, with the reason), the expected verdicts, the minimal subset additions, and sizes to pre-register. Measure simple_sat vs picosat_elixir on a few generated 3-SAT instances and on Ash-shaped formulas if you can derive them from simple_sat's tests; mark measured vs quoted and note the machine was not quiet.

## Method

Primary sources: the two repositories and Hex packages (download counts via the Hex API), Ash's code that calls the solver (ash's Ash.SatSolver module), PicoSAT's paper/README for the algorithm, this repo's CONTEXT.md, README and docs/research/*.md for the subset and the catalog rules.

Output: branch research/sat-solver, docs/research/sat-solver.md, in the format of docs/research/nif-workloads.md.

comments.text: Recommendation: a SAT solver is a good defk example as a bounded CDCL kernel, filed as a defk-52v rewrite (Tier 1 by constructs, Tier 2 by size), anchored on picosat_elixir (NIF, normal scheduler, measured 3.9 s scheduler block at n=300) and simple_sat (pure Elixir, no unit propagation, exponential: first-pass only), and measured on Ash's real job in batch form: Crux.satisfying_scenarios (1 + V solves per scenario, 7 to 1,548 calls per authorization on Ash-shaped formulas) run in one kernel call. Per call, Ash formulas are 6-109 vars / 13-371 clauses and picosat solves them in 4-82 us, as cheap as packing the CNF (~31 us), so a per-call drop-in is a guidance entry expected marginal at P=4 (~27 vars) and good (provisional) only at P=12 (~105 vars). Pre-registered expected verdicts vs an optimized Elixir solver: S1 per-call P=4 marginal; S2 per-call P=12 good (provisional); S3 batch scenarios P=12 good (Crux+Elixir DPLL 588-953 ms vs Crux+picosat 101-108 ms); S4 random 3-SAT n=200 ratio 4.26 good; S5 responsiveness at n=300 reported beside. Agreement: kernel vs Elixir mode exact (pinned tie-breaks, deterministic schedule); vs anchors same SAT/UNSAT status plus a model that satisfies every clause; batch scenarios as an equivalent cover, since Crux's scenario sets differ by solver (measured). Minimal additions: defk-n4r.4 (helpers write arrays by returning them; suggest a single state arena), then defk-ivt; defk-w38 optional; learned clauses fit a fixed alloc'd arena with PicoSAT-style reduce, so defk-cmr, defk-n4r.3 and defk-sve are not needed. Branch research/sat-solver, file docs/research/sat-solver.md (commit 8cfe5f3).
Filed: defk-52v.15 (bounded CDCL kernel, Tier 2 under defk-52v) and defk-9p6.25 (per-call guidance entry). Research branch research/sat-solver unmerged, as the other research branches.

title: Is a SAT solver a good defk example: simple_sat's job, or a picosat reimplementation?
